source.title: PRISM: Parametrically Refactoring Inference for Speculative Sampling Draft Models
source.authors: Xuliang Wang; Yuetao Chen; Maochan Zhen; Fang Liu; Xinzhou Zheng; Xingwu Liu; Hong Xu; Ming Li

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports scaling results for speculative-decoding drafter acceptance length, not held-out language-model pretraining loss or the parameter/token/compute relationships in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's own scaling experiments vary drafter training-data volume and measure acceptance length. This is a related but different outcome from the losses or downstream performance named in V1–V7, so these findings are recorded as none-version results. It does not report a loss-scaling sweep or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Table 4–5 acceptance-length and throughput comparisons, and other inference-speed results, are not rows because they do not report the claimed scaling behavior.
record.test_reason: The paper's 'scaling law' section varies drafter training data (100k–800k samples) and reports acceptance length for speculative-decoding drafters. It reports no held-out loss, no power-law fit, no extrapolation and no compute-optimal allocation. Acceptance length is a different construct from the loss or downstream-task performance the versions name, and the scaling sweep mainly serves to compare the authors' own drafter architecture with baselines. So it does not test V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors claim to 'verify scaling law for draft models' and to show that PRISM scales more effectively with data. This concerns acceptance length of speculative-decoding drafters, not loss.
record.recipe_differences: The paper varies training-data volume for speculative-decoding drafters and measures acceptance length; the claim concerns held-out pretraining loss and parameter, token, and compute scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported scaling outcomes differ by drafter architecture and training-data volume; the paper also notes differing behavior across benchmarks and sampling settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Drafter acceptance length rises with training-data volume. EAGLE-2 and HASS plateau after about 400k samples, while PRISM keeps improving past 600k.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Speculative-decoding drafter acceptance length scales with training data, and the saturation point depends on drafter architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: PRISM beats EAGLE-3 at low data volume, and the two converge at higher volume.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Drafter data efficiency differs by architecture, but the gap may close as data grows.

fits_no_version.finding: Naively stacking two transformer layers scales worse in acceptance length than PRISM's step-specialized parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Drafter architecture affects how acceptance length scales with training data.

record.problems: The reported scaling outcomes are for acceptance length rather than loss; the scaling curves are presented in figures, and the text does not state uncertainty estimates for them. The authors characterize the dataset as limited in complexity when explaining the P RISM–EAGLE-3 convergence.
record.rows_left_out: Individual plotted curves and values for each benchmark and sampling setting in Figures 4–6 were not transcribed; the rows record only the outcomes the accompanying text states. Table 4–5 throughput and acceptance-length comparisons were left out because they are not reported as scaling results.

untested.parts: All: no held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no fits and no extrapolation.
All: no loss comparison across shapes at fixed parameter count.
All: drafter acceptance length is not a power-law fit of loss in another regime.
All: no downstream task performance versus scale or loss.
All: no exponent fitting; the plateaus are in acceptance length, not loss.

record.verdict_notes: The paper uses 'scaling laws' loosely, meaning that more drafter training data improves acceptance length. It fits no functional form and reports no uncertainty. Training epochs differ by dataset size ('more epochs... for smaller datasets'), which confounds the data-volume sweep. Table 4–5 results are rightly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether small-run loss fits predict much larger-run losses.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and how it changes with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices on loss at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds for loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream task performance scaling or prediction from pretraining loss.
Dependence of the claimed loss-law exponents or compute-optimal split on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: P RISM
rows.operation_detail: Compared acceptance length across training-data volumes.
rows.measure: Acceptance length as training-data volume increases
rows.value: P RISM demonstrates a big advantage in acceptance length across all tested data scales and still shows potential to scale with more than 600,000 samples.
rows.note: The stated outcome concerns drafter acceptance length, not held-out pretraining loss.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method (PRISM) against baselines on acceptance length, not a loss-scaling result. The 'observed' state has no version to be judged against.

rows.subject: EAGLE-2
rows.operation_detail: Compared acceptance length across training-data volumes.
rows.measure: Acceptance length as training-data volume increases
rows.value: Performance begins to plateau after 400,000 samples.
rows.note: The paper describes a plateau in this drafter's acceptance-length curve.
rows.check: The EAGLE-2 plateau after 400k samples is in acceptance length, not loss. The 'partial' state has no version referent.

rows.subject: HASS
rows.operation_detail: Compared acceptance length across training-data volumes.
rows.measure: Acceptance length as training-data volume increases
rows.value: Performance begins to plateau after 400,000 samples.
rows.note: The paper describes a plateau in this drafter's acceptance-length curve.
rows.check: The HASS plateau after 400k samples is in acceptance length, not loss. The 'partial' state has no version referent.

rows.subject: P RISM
rows.operation_detail: Compared acceptance length across training-data volumes with EAGLE-3.
rows.measure: Acceptance length as training-data volume increases
rows.value: P RISM outperforms EAGLE-3 with relatively small amounts of data; as data volume increases, both methods converge to the same acceptance length.
rows.note: The reported measure is acceptance length, not the loss named by the claim.
rows.check: This is an own-method versus baseline (EAGLE-3) comparison. The authors attribute the convergence to limited dataset complexity.

rows.subject: EAGLE-3
rows.operation_detail: Compared acceptance length across training-data volumes with P RISM.
rows.measure: Acceptance length as training-data volume increases
rows.value: As data volume increases, EAGLE-3 and P RISM converge to the same acceptance length.
rows.note: The paper attributes the convergence to the limited complexity of its dataset.
rows.check: This duplicates r4 from the comparator's side. It is an own-method comparison, not a scaling-law test.

rows.subject: Model directly stacking two transformers
rows.operation_detail: Compared acceptance-length scaling with P RISM using the same context alignment and dataset.
rows.measure: Acceptance length and its change with training-data volume
rows.value: The ablation model predicts and scales considerably worse than P RISM.
rows.note: This comparison concerns drafter acceptance length and architecture, not held-out pretraining loss.
rows.check: This is an ablation of the authors' own architecture against stacked transformers. The target model is not stated in the text and no numbers are given.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
